## Objective

- Set up a repository on GitHub
- Prepare your project for migration to GitHub
- Check that the project runs in its new location

Note: This session assumes familiarity with the basics of GitHub


## Before Getting Started

- **Important:** If the team is moving shared code to GitHub, everyone who edits that code should work from the GitHub clone. Keeping separate active copies in GitHub and OneDrive can lead to confusion and lost changes.
- This guide assumes that your files are currently stored and shared through OneDrive. The steps are similar for other syncing services, such as SharePoint or Dropbox, and for projects shared on a network drive or another shared location.


# Section 1: Request a GitHub Repository {background-color="#530153"}

## Request a GitHub Repository

### Repo requirement

* You need a repository under one of the World Bank's GitHub accounts. If you already have one, skip to Section 2.
* If not, follow the steps in this section to request one.

## Request a repo

Request a new repository by sending this email to [dimeanalytics@worldbank.org](mailto:dimeanalytics@worldbank.org), unless you already have a repository to use. Copy and fill in this information in the email:

::: {.callout-tip title="Repo Request Email template"}

**Repository Name**:<br>
**Repository Description** _(max 350 characters)_:<br>
**GitHub Account** (`dime-worldbank` (DECDI) or `worldbank` (everyone else)):<br>
**Will you use an existing team** _(yes/no)_:<br>
**DIME GitHub Team Name** (_existing team or team to be created_):<br>
**Your GitHub Username**: <br>

:::


## Information neeed to request a GitHub Repository

### Description
A brief "_about_" section for your repository. GitHub limits descriptions to 350 characters. 

Here are some good examples to follow: [ietoolkit](https://github.com/worldbank/ietoolkit/), [dia-toolkit](https://github.com/worldbank/dia-toolkit/), or [moz-proirri-savings](https://github.com/dime-worldbank/moz-proirri-savings).

### Repo Name
A good repo name is descriptive but also works well as a URL. Here are specific guidelines:
* Use only lowercase letters (`a-z`), numbers (`0-9`), and hyphens (`-`). Avoid spaces, underscores, uppercase letters, and other special characters for readable, portable repository names.
* Do not start the name with a number. Use hyphens to separate words.
* Avoid long repository names to keep URLs manageable and easy to share.

[See here for example names on the DECDI account](https://github.com/orgs/dime-worldbank/repositories).

## GitHub Team 

- Repository access is given at team-level (not individuals) when the repo is created. 
- Each GitHub team will designate at least one "team maintainer" who can manage membership, which grants/revokes access to the team's repositories. Best practice is to have two maintainers.
- Read more about GitHub Teams and why we use them [here](https://github.com/dime-worldbank/dime-account-admin/blob/main/resources/why-use-teams.md).

### Use a single team for multiple repositories
* GitHub teams can be assigned to one or more repositories. 
* When possible, use an existing team for a new repository 
    * Ex. a second repository is created for the same project, use the same team as the first repository. 
* This reduces workload for both the project team and the GitHub account administrators.

### Create a new team if needed
* If no existing team is suitable, a new team can be created. 
* When naming a new team, follow the repository naming conventions above. 
* Do not use the exact same name for the team as for the repository. You can use `<repo-name>-team` if you want similar names.



# Section 2: Move Files {background-color="#530153"}

## Clone Your Repository

* Wait for confirmation that your repository has been created.
* Clone the repository to your computer and open the clone folder.

### Warning!!

In some steps on the next slide you will delete files from your computer. If you have followed the instructions correctly, the files should be backed up in either OneDrive or GitHub. 

However, move slowly through these slides and ask the helpers if you are unsure about any step. It is better to ask too often than to risk losing files.

## Step 1: Make Sure You Have a Good `.gitignore`
* Before moving on, check that the repository has a useful `.gitignore` file. Review it and add project-specific rules as needed; do not assume the defaults cover every file you need to exclude.

### Why Use a `.gitignore` File

Some files should not be committed to GitHub, for reasons of:

- Efficiency: don't add large or frequently updated binary files (for example,`.dta`, `.doc`, `.pdf`, `.xls` etc.) These can make a repository slower and take up 100s of GB on each persons computer. 
- Data privacy: GitHub is not approved for confidential data (regardless if your repository is private or public).

**Note:** Files not shared on GitHub can continue to be shared through OneDrive.

### Use a template

- Your repository may already include a `.gitignore` template. 
- If not, you can start with the [Impact Analytics template](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/worldbank/dime-github-trainings/refs/heads/main/GitHub-resources/DIME-GitHub-Templates/gitignore_template.txt) and modify if needed (you probably don't need to). 
- To use the template, copy the content from the link above into a new `.gitignore` file in your repository.

## Step 2: Copy Files into the Clone

1. First make sure the `.gitignore` file is present in your clone on your computer.
2. Copy the code or data work folder from your existing project into the clone. Make sure to **copy, not move or cut and paste, the files**. Wait for the copy to finish.
    - If the project is too large to copy in one go, copy files selectively. Keep the original project intact and check that all required files and folder paths are included.
3. Then use GitHub Desktop to review the files shown as ready to commit.
  - Make sure that only files you want to track on GitHub are included in each commit. If needed, update the `.gitignore` file to exclude files you do not want to commit.
  - Check the files carefully to ensure no confidential or identifying information is being sent to GitHub.
  - Review files folder by folder and commit in manageable groups rather than committing everything at once.

## Step 3: Verify Ignored Files

Check that the `.gitignore` rules are not excluding files that should be tracked on GitHub. This is a temporary check; do not commit while the file is removed.

1. In the clone, temporarily remove the `.gitignore` file.
2. In GitHub Desktop, review the additional files that become visible. **Do not commit them**. 
3. Verify that each file in the staging area should remain outside GitHub (often data or generated files).
4. Restore the `.gitignore` file in GitHub Desktop by discarding its deletion. 

If a file that should be tracked was ignored, restore the `.gitignore` file, update the rules and commit that file. Repeat as necessary.

## Step 4: Test a Clean Clone

Before testing a clean clone, confirm that the original project is intact and that the commits you need have been pushed to GitHub. Do not delete your only copy of any files or discard uncommitted work.

- Anyone cloning the repository gets the files committed and pushed to GitHub, not uncommitted local files. 
- To create a clean clone, delete your clone and re-clone the repository from GitHub.
- Open that clean clone and check that the project has the expected files. 
- The next section helps you verify the project code runs as intended. 

Next, update code paths and address folders that Git does not otherwise represent. 

# Section 3: Make Code Work in its new location {background-color="#530153"}

## Update Folder Paths in Code - Stata (1/3)

When code and other project files are all stored in OneDrive, a main script may need only one root path:

```stata
global onedrive "C:\Users\WB123456\OneDrive - WBG\Projects\my-agriculture-project"
```

When code is shared in GitHub and other files remain in OneDrive, you will need to define two root paths:

```stata
global onedrive "C:\Users\WB123456\OneDrive - WBG\Projects\my-agriculture-project"
global clone    "C:/Users/WB123456/github/my-agriculture-project"
```

## Code Points to Different Locations - Stata (2/3)

Code in the clone and data in OneDrive use different roots. For example, in Stata:

```stata
* Define globals
global onedrive "C:/Users/username/OneDrive - WBG/Projects/my-agriculture-project"
global clone    "C:/Users/username/Documents/GitHub/my-agriculture-project"

* Open data from OneDrive
use "${onedrive}/Baseline/data/hh_data_deidentified.dta", clear

* Run analysis code from the clone
do "${clone}/Baseline/dofiles/hh_analysis.do"
```

## Add the Clone Folder Path - Stata (3/3)

1. In main scripts, define both the OneDrive root and the clone root.

```stata
if ${user} == 1 {
  global onedrive "C:/Users/username/OneDrive/DIME Analytics"
  global clone    "C:/Users/username/Documents/GitHub/dimeanalytics"
}
```
2. Update other globals so data paths point to OneDrive and code paths point to the clone. Put outputs in the clone only when they are appropriate to track (plain-text formats such as `.tex`/`.qmd` or small image files); otherwise keep them in OneDrive and exclude them from Git.

```stata
global Baseline_od  "${onedrive}/Baseline"
global Baseline     "${clone}/Baseline"
global Baseline_dt  "${Baseline_od}/DataSets"
global Baseline_do  "${Baseline}/Dofiles"
global Baseline_out "${Baseline}/Output"
```

## Update Folder Paths in Code - R (1/3)

In R, you do not need to define a root path for the clone. An **RStudio Project** in the clone folder, together with the [`here`](https://here.r-lib.org/) package, finds it for you.

### Create a Project in your clone (once)

1. In RStudio: **File > Open Project > New Project > Existing Directory**
2. Browse to your GitHub clone folder and click **Create Project**
3. Commit the new `.Rproj` file so everyone who clones gets it

## Code Points to Different Locations - R (2/3)

**If everything is in the clone**, you are good to go. Open the `.Rproj` and build paths with `here()`. They will work on every computer.

```r
library(here)

source(here("Baseline", "code", "hh_analysis.R"))
```

**If data stays in OneDrive**, add one variable for its location and use it for data only:

```r
library(here)

# Location of the project data in OneDrive (edit to match your computer)
onedrive <- "C:/Users/WB123456/OneDrive - WBG/Projects/my-agriculture-project"

# Open data from OneDrive
hh_data <- haven::read_dta(file.path(onedrive, "Baseline", "data", "hh_data_deidentified.dta"))

# Run analysis code from the clone
source(here("Baseline", "code", "hh_analysis.R"))
```

## Add the Clone Folder Path - R (3/3)

1. Always open the project by double-clicking the `.Rproj` file. `here()` uses it to find the clone root.
2. Define the `onedrive` variable **once**, at the top of your main script. Each person edits this one line to match their own computer.
3. Build all other paths from these two roots. Data goes with `onedrive`, code and tracked outputs go with `here()`.

```r
onedrive <- "C:/Users/WB123456/OneDrive - WBG/Projects/my-agriculture-project"

baseline_dt  <- file.path(onedrive, "Baseline", "data")
baseline_do  <- here("Baseline", "code")
baseline_out <- here("Baseline", "output")
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Two things to avoid"}
- **Do not use `setwd()`.** It hard-codes a path that only works on your computer. `here()` makes it unnecessary.
- **Use `/` in paths, not a single `\`.**
:::

## Other languages 

In other languages, define separate roots for OneDrive and the clone, then build file paths from the appropriate root. Keep data and other files that should not be tracked outside the clone.

Ask a helper if you are unsure how to apply this approach in your programming language.


# Section 4: Automatically Fix the Empty-Folder Issue {background-color="#530153"}

## Why Empty Folders Are Not Shared

- Git tracks files, not folders by themselves.
- A file's path is part of its name to Git. For example, `src/ado_files/iebaltab.ado` includes its folder path.
- A tracked file causes its containing folder and parent folders to appear in a clone.
- A folder with no tracked files is not represented in Git, even if it exists in your personal clone.

## Empty Folders: 

### The Problem

If a folder contains only files ignored by Git (for example, generated `.png` files), the folder will not be present in a fresh clone. Code that expects to write to that folder may then fail.

### The Solution - Two options

1. Before saving a file, have the code check whether the target folder exists and create it if necessary. Most languages provide a way to do this, but easier in languages with advanced file system utilities, such as Python.

2. Add a placeholder file such as `README.md` to folders that need to exist in the clone but contain no other files tracked by Git. Git tracks the placeholder, so it also represents the folder path. See the `iegitaddmd` command ([documentation](https://worldbank.github.io/ietoolkit/reference/iegitaddmd.html)) for a utility that can do this.

# Section 5: Delete Code from OneDrive {background-color="#530153"}

## Delete code from previous location once GitHub migration is complete and verified

Do this step only after the GitHub clone has been checked and the team is ready to use it as the shared code location. 

Keep a backup of anything that is not committed to GitHub.

- Maintaining two active copies of the code can cause confusion and lead to lost changes.
- GitHub should become the source of truth for shared code.
- It is reasonable to wait while testing the migration, but avoid maintaining two active copies longer than necessary.
